title: A New Heart and a New Spirit
summary: Ezekiel speaks to the ruined mountains of Israel, promising that they will bear fruit again for a people coming home and that the nations who mocked them will bear their own reproach. God then explains why Israel was scattered and why he will restore it: not because they deserve it, but for the sake of his holy name. He promises to gather them, cleanse them with clean water, replace their heart of stone with a heart of flesh, and put his own Spirit within them.
story: Chapter 35 condemned Mount Seir; chapter 36 answers it by addressing the mountains of Israel with hope. The land that enemies claimed, and that had seemed to devour its own inhabitants, will be tilled, sown, and filled with people. But the chapter goes deeper than a return to real estate. Ezekiel had spent years showing that Israel's problem was its heart: idolatry, bloodshed, and a stubbornness no warning could cure. Here God promises to solve that problem himself. This is the theological center of the restoration section, and it prepares directly for the vision of dry bones given breath in chapter 37.
historical:
These oracles belong to the years after Jerusalem's fall in 587 or 586 BC. The land of Judah was depopulated, many towns lay in ruins, and neighboring peoples, especially Edom, had moved into its southern territory (verse 5). The exiles in Babylonia faced a theological crisis as sharp as the political one. In the ancient world a nation's defeat was commonly taken as its god's defeat, so the nations could say, as verse 20 puts it, "These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land."

The return began about fifty years later, after Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed exiled peoples to return home (Ezra 1). The returning community rebuilt the temple and resettled parts of Judah, a partial but real fulfillment of the chapter's promise of rebuilt cities. Whether that return exhausts the promise of a new heart and God's Spirit within is a question the rest of the Bible takes up.
cultural:
Verse 17 compares Israel's conduct to the ritual impurity of menstruation, a comparison that sounds harsh to modern ears. In Israel's purity laws (Leviticus 15:19-24), menstruation made a woman ritually unclean for a time; it was not a sin, but it meant separation from holy things. Ezekiel, a priest, uses that category to say that Israel's sins made the land unfit for God's presence, like a defilement that required separation.

The cleansing of verse 25 also draws on priestly practice. Water was sprinkled for purification from contact with death (Numbers 19:17-19), and sprinkling with blood or water marked people and objects as clean and consecrated. In the ancient Near East the heart was the center of thought, will, and moral choice, not mainly of emotion. A heart of stone is a mind and will that cannot respond; a heart of flesh is one that is alive and responsive to God. The spirit (ruach, also wind and breath) was the animating power of life.
literary: The chapter has two main parts. Verses 1 to 15 are an oracle to the mountains of Israel, deliberately mirroring chapter 35's oracle to Mount Seir. It piles up "therefore" clauses and addresses the land directly: mountains, hills, ravines, and valleys. Verses 16 to 38 turn to the people and are built as an argument: the history of defilement (verses 16 to 21), God's motive (verses 22 to 23), the program of restoration (verses 24 to 30), Israel's response of shame (verses 31 to 32), and the rebuilding of the land (verses 33 to 38). The phrase "not for your sake" frames the central promise (verses 22 and 32), so that the grace of verses 24 to 28 sits inside a reminder that it is undeserved.

outline.t: The mountains of Israel and the nations' reproach
The land will be fruitful and inhabited again
Why Israel was scattered: a defiled land and a profaned name
For the sake of God's holy name
Gathered, cleansed, given a new heart and God's Spirit
Ruins rebuilt, a land like Eden

doctrines.note: "I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes" (verse 27). The Spirit is promised not merely as occasional power for prophets and leaders but as God's presence within his whole people, enabling the obedience the law required and they could not give.

Every verb in verses 24 to 29 has God as its subject: I will take, gather, bring, sprinkle, cleanse, give, remove, put, cause, save. Restoration is God's work from start to finish, including the new heart that makes a faithful response possible.

God acts "for My holy name" (verse 22). His name is his revealed character, and Israel's exile had made him look weak or faithless before the nations. He restores his people to show the truth about himself.
"You will be My people, and I will be your God" (verse 28) restates the covenant bond. The new heart and Spirit are the means by which that bond, broken by Israel's unfaithfulness, will finally hold.

words.note: Lev, heart. In Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of understanding, decision, and loyalty. God promises to replace a heart that is hard as stone with a heart of flesh, a living one able to respond.
Ruach, spirit, breath, wind. In verse 26 it names a new inner disposition; in verse 27 it is God's own Spirit. The same word will carry the vision of chapter 37, where breath enters the dry bones.
Chadash, new. A new heart and a new spirit; the word recalls Jeremiah's new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). The newness is not a repair of the old but a gift from outside.
Chalal, to profane, to treat as common what is holy. Five times in the chapter. Israel profaned God's name among the nations, and God acts to show its holiness again.

christ: The New Testament reads this promise as fulfilled in the gift of the Spirit through Christ. When Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless born of water and the Spirit, and chides him as Israel's teacher for not understanding (John 3:5-10), many interpreters hear Ezekiel 36:25-27, with its clean water and new spirit, in the background. Paul describes believers as a letter written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:3), an echo of both Ezekiel and Jeremiah. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's matching new covenant promise and says Christ is its mediator (Hebrews 8:6-13). The pattern of the chapter, a people cleansed and renewed not for their own sake but for God's glory, is also the pattern of the gospel: salvation by grace, not by works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8-9).

hard.q: Who is this promise for: the Jews who returned from Babylon, the church, or a future restoration of Israel?
hard.a: Christians read the chapter in several ways. Almost all agree that the return from Babylon after 539 BC was a real first fulfillment of the promise to rebuild the ruins and resettle the land, and that the returned community did not yet have the new heart the chapter describes. Many Christian interpreters, especially in Reformed and covenant traditions, see the promise of cleansing and the Spirit fulfilled in the new covenant community of Jews and Gentiles in Christ, with the land promise widened into the renewed creation. Dispensational interpreters, and others who expect a future national restoration of Israel (often reading Romans 11:25-27 alongside this chapter), hold that the promise will also be fulfilled for ethnic Israel, including in the land, when the Jewish people as a whole turn to Christ. Jewish interpreters read it as God's pledge to the Jewish people that still awaits completion. These are second-order questions among Christians, and the chapter itself stays focused on what all readers share: God will act for his name, and the new heart is his gift.

questions: God says he will act "not for your sake" but for his name. Is that humbling, comforting, or both? Why?
What would it look like in your life for a heart of stone to become a heart of flesh?
Verse 31 says the restored people will remember their evil ways and loathe them. Why does real restoration bring a clearer sense of sin rather than a weaker one?
